mcq.q: Which hypothesis did Freeman and colleagues (2014) set out to test?
o: The hypothesis that the number of students in a class has no effect at all on results
The hypothesis that standardized tests measure every kind of student ability
The hypothesis that lecturing maximizes learning and course performance
The hypothesis that group study is always less effective than each student studying alone
mcq.e: The abstract: "To test the hypothesis that lecturing maximizes learning and course performance, we metaanalyzed 225 studies".

mcq.q: How many studies did the meta-analysis pool, and in which field?
o: 67 studies of all subjects at the primary and lower secondary school level
52 studies of language and literature courses at the upper secondary school level
225 studies of undergraduate science, technology, engineering
158 studies of social science courses at the postgraduate level
mcq.e: The paper: "we metaanalyzed 225 studies... comparing student performance in undergraduate science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) courses".

mcq.q: Which two conditions did the pooled studies compare?
o: Traditional lecturing versus courses with at least some active learning
Classes of strong students versus classes of weak students on the same course
Face-to-face classes versus fully online classes with no instructor at all
Classes with experienced instructors versus classes with brand-new instructors
mcq.e: The paper: "courses with at least some active learning versus traditional lecturing".

mcq.q: How does the paper define active learning?
o: Students studying alone at home from textbooks without needing to attend class
It engages students in learning through activities and/or discussion in class instead of passively listening to an expert, emphasizes higher-order thinking and often involves group work
Students watching lecture videos before class and handing in individual homework
Students listening to the instructor speak continuously and then taking a short quiz
mcq.e: The definition: "Active learning engages students in the process of learning through activities and/or discussion in class, as opposed to passively listening to an expert. It emphasizes higher-order thinking and often involves group work."

mcq.q: How did the authors build the definition of active learning?
o: By asking a panel of ten experts to vote on a definition
By quoting a single definition from a widely used education dictionary
By taking the definition from the education law of the United States and Canada
By collecting written definitions from 338 seminar audience members
mcq.e: The paper: "we collected written definitions from 338 audience members, before biology departmental seminars... We then coded elements in the responses".

mcq.q: How is traditional lecturing defined (following Bligh)?
o: A session in which students discuss in groups continuously while the teacher only observes
A recorded session that students can watch again many times at home after class
Continuous exposition by the teacher, with student activity limited to note taking or occasional unprompted questions
A session with many individual practice tasks that the teacher grades right away
mcq.e: The paper: "traditional lecturing as '...continuous exposition by the teacher.' Under this definition, student activity was assumed to be limited to taking notes and/or asking occasional and unprompted questions of the instructor."

mcq.q: How varied were the active learning interventions?
o: Only the instructor asking questions and calling on students one by one
Only weekly quizzes so that students review what they learned earlier
Only one kind: small-group discussion lasting the whole class period
From occasional group problem-solving, in-class worksheets
mcq.e: The paper: "approaches as diverse as occasional group problem-solving, worksheets or tutorials completed during class, use of personal response systems with or without peer instruction, and studio or workshop course designs."

mcq.q: What were the two outcome variables?
o: Hours of self-study and number of times students spoke in class
Student satisfaction and instructor satisfaction with the class
Income after graduation and time needed to find a job
Scores on identical or equivalent assessments, and failure rates
mcq.e: The paper: "(i) scores on identical or formally equivalent examinations, concept inventories, or other assessments; or (ii) failure rates".

mcq.q: How is the failure (DFW) rate usually measured?
o: The percentage of students who did not submit the final project of the course
The percentage of students scoring below the class average in that course
The percentage of students absent from more than half of the class sessions
The percentage of students receiving a D or F or withdrawing from the course
mcq.e: The paper: "failure rates, usually measured as the percentage of students receiving a D or F grade or withdrawing from the course in question (DFW rate)."

mcq.q: Which part of course design did the analysis focus on?
o: Design of class sessions, not laboratories or homework assignments
Laboratory work and take-home projects of the students
The whole degree program made of many courses in sequence
The exam and grading system of the entire university
mcq.e: The paper: "we focused on the design of class sessions—as opposed to laboratories, homework assignments, or other exercises."

mcq.q: What was the pooled effect on exam scores and other assessments?
o: 0.20 standard deviations, from 225 studies
0.47 standard deviations, from 158 studies
0.64 standard deviations, from 158 studies
1.95 standard deviations, from 67 studies
mcq.e: The paper: "a weighted standardized mean difference of 0.47 (Z = 9.781, P << 0.001)", from n = 158 studies.

mcq.q: What does 0.47 mean in practice?
o: 47% of active-learning students reached the maximum score on the final exam
Students under active learning scored 47% higher than students under lecturing
Student performance rose by just under half a standard deviation under active learning compared with lecturing
Scores rose by exactly 0.47 points on a ten-point scale in every course
mcq.e: The paper: "on average, student performance increased by just under half a SD with active learning compared with lecturing."

mcq.q: What was the odds ratio for failing under traditional lecturing?
o: 1.95, from 67 studies
1.5, from 225 studies
0.47, from 158 studies
3.5, from 29 studies
mcq.e: The paper: "The overall mean effect size for failure rate was an odds ratio of 1.95 (Z = 10.4, P << 0.001)", n = 67.

mcq.q: What risk ratio is an odds ratio of 1.95 equivalent to, and what does it mean?
o: A risk ratio of 1.95: students in lecture courses are almost twice as likely to fail
A risk ratio of 1.5: students in lecture courses are 1.5 times as likely to fail as those in active courses
A risk ratio of 0.64: students in lecture courses are less likely to fail than active students
A risk ratio of 1.0: the two kinds of class have identical failure rates statistically
mcq.e: The paper: "This odds ratio is equivalent to a risk ratio of 1.5, meaning that on average, students in traditional lecture courses are 1.5 times more likely to fail than students in courses with active learning."

mcq.q: What were the average failure rates in the two kinds of class?
o: 47% in active learning classes and 95% in lecture classes
21.8% in active learning classes and 33.8% in lecture classes
33.8% in active learning classes and 21.8% in lecture classes
12% in active learning classes and 55% in lecture classes
mcq.e: The paper: "Average failure rates were 21.8% under active learning but 33.8% under traditional lecturing".

mcq.q: The difference in failure rates represents what percentage increase?
o: A 12% increase over the failure rate in active learning classes
A 55% increase over the failure rate in active learning classes
A 95% increase over the failure rate in active learning classes
A 47% increase over the failure rate in active learning classes
mcq.e: The paper: "a difference that represents a 55% increase". Check: (33.8 − 21.8)/21.8 is about 0.55.

mcq.q: What is the absolute difference between 33.8% and 21.8%?
o: 6 percentage points
21.8 percentage points
12 percentage points
55 percentage points
mcq.e: 33.8 minus 21.8 is 12; the paper also gives "The mean change (12%)" in Fig. 1.

mcq.q: By about how much do mean exam scores rise under active learning, per the authors' conversion?
o: About 1%, translating to 0.01 points in the final grade
About 21%, translating to 2 points in the final grade
About 47%, translating to 3 points in the final grade
About 6%, translating to 0.3 points in the final grade
mcq.e: The paper: "a change of 0.47 SDs would produce an increase of about 6% in average examination scores and would translate to a 0.3 point increase in average final grade."

mcq.q: On a letter grade system, what happens to median grades in the analyzed courses?
o: They would rise from B− to B or from B to B+
They would not change since a 0.3-point rise is too small to matter
They would fall from B to B− in most of the analyzed courses
They would rise from C to A in every analyzed course
mcq.e: The paper: "medians in the courses analyzed would rise from a B− to a B or from a B to a B+."

mcq.q: At what percentile would a student at the 50th percentile under lecturing land under active learning?
o: The 68th percentile
The 95th percentile
The 55th percentile
The 47th percentile
mcq.e: The paper: "Students performing in the 50th percentile of a class based on traditional lecturing would, under active learning, move to the 68th percentile of that class".

mcq.q: Why does about 0.68 for a 0.47 SD shift agree with the 68th percentile?
o: Because 68 is a fixed share of students who earn a B in every class
Because the percentile always equals twice the effect size in any data
Under a normal distribution, shifting by 0.47 SD moves someone from the 50th to about the 68th percentile
Because 0.47 times 100 plus 21 gives exactly 68 by the paper's formula
mcq.e: The paper converts the effect to percentiles; under a normal distribution the area up to 0.47 SD is about 0.68 (my own calculation note).

mcq.q: How does the undergraduate active learning effect compare with K–12 interventions?
o: It cannot be compared because K–12 has no reviews of effect sizes
It appears larger: K–12 averages 0.39 with researcher-developed tests
It is exactly equal for every type of test in both K–12 and university
It is much smaller: K–12 averages 1.00 with researcher-developed tests

o: These studies certainly were stopped because active learning harmed students
These studies cannot be compared with medicine since P exceeded 0.05 throughout
These studies were randomized medical trials, so they are fully comparable
These studies might have been stopped for benefit (mean relative risk 0.64)

mcq.q: Of the 29,300 students in the 67 lecture sections with failure data, about how many would have failed less under active learning?
o: About 3,516 students
About 12,000 students
About 29,300 students
About 350 students

mcq.q: What tuition savings did the authors estimate for the study population?
o: About US$35,000
Over US$3.5 million
Over US$21 million
About US$350

mcq.q: What is the STEM "pipeline problem" mentioned?
o: Under 40% of US students entering with STEM interest
Universities do not have enough STEM faculty to open classes for students
Too many STEM students graduate, so there are not enough jobs for all of them
STEM students often switch to other majors because tuition is too high

o: A 33% increase in STEM bachelor's degrees completed per year
A 50% rise in STEM tuition to fund reform of teaching
A 33% cut in the number of traditional lecture courses in universities
A requirement that every STEM instructor use active learning within a year

mcq.q: What did the analysis by STEM discipline show?
o: Effects differed greatly among disciplines with P below 0.001
Only mathematics showed a significant effect while the other disciplines did not
No statistically significant variation among disciplines in exam scores or failure rates
Only biology showed a significant effect while the other disciplines did not

o: Only concept inventories showed an effect while instructor exams did not
They were smaller for instructor-written exams than for concept inventories
They were equal, since both measure exactly the same cognitive skill in students
They were larger for instructor-written exams than for concept inventories in every study

Concept inventories are easier, so every student scores highly in the same way

Class size had no influence and all three sizes gave equal effects
The effect was largest in classes of 50 or fewer, but still significant in medium
The effect was significant only in medium classes of 51 to 110 students

o: Medium: 10 to 30 students; large: over 30 students
Medium: 20 to 50 students; large: over 50 students
Medium: 100 to 200 students; large: over 200 students

o: No significant difference between majors and nonmajors, or between introductory
Active learning worked only in courses for majors and not in courses for nonmajors
The effect in upper-division courses was double that in introductory courses everywhere
Active learning worked only in introductory courses and not in upper-division courses

mcq.q: What is publication bias in this context?
o: The tendency of journals to publish only studies by famous authors
The tendency of authors to publish the same study in many different journals
The tendency for studies with large effects not to be published in journals
The tendency for studies with low effect sizes to remain unpublished

Randomized studies gave clearly larger effects than quasi-random studies
Only randomized studies gave statistically significant effects in the data
No difference (Q = 2.097, P = 0.553): random assignment gave results indistinguishable from quasi-random designs

mcq.e: Table 1: "Randomized assignment or crossover design: 16, 0.514".

mcq.q: How does 0.47 compare with earlier meta-analyses in subsets of STEM?
o: It is much smaller than the 1.00 in earlier meta-analyses of other disciplines
It cannot be compared since earlier meta-analyses used entirely different units
It is almost identical to the 0.50 and 0.51 in earlier meta-analyses
It is much larger than the 0.10 in earlier meta-analyses of other disciplines

Struggling students drop courses more often
Because lecture classes always contain better students than active learning classes
Because exams in active learning classes are harder than exams in lecture classes

o: Whether lecturing is still used at universities
Whether active learning raises students' tuition
Whether the effect would hold
Whether students prefer active learning over lecturing
mcq.e: The paper: "The instructors who implemented active learning in these studies did so as volunteers. It is an open question whether student performance would increase as much if all faculty were required to implement active learning approaches."

o: Lack of data, though time ranged from 10 to 15% of class time to lecture-free studio courses
Because the studies reported no exam scores for the participating students
Because all studies used exactly the same intensity of 50% of class time
Because the intensity of active learning cannot be measured in any classroom

mcq.q: What is the "second-generation research" the authors propose?

Studying only fully online classes to see whether students learn differently
Repeating the old experiments with bigger samples to raise statistical reliability
Using educational psychology and cognitive science to design courses, then testing

o: Because lecture control groups always have better students than active groups
Because the results show active learning is superior
Because traditional lecturing has been banned in every US university
Because lecture control groups are too expensive to organize in studies
mcq.e: The paper: "it is reasonable to raise concerns about the continued use of traditional lecturing as a control in future experiments. Instead, it may be more productive to focus on... 'second-generation research'."

mcq.q: For which student groups does recent work suggest disproportionate benefits from active learning?
o: The top students of the class at highly ranked universities across the country
Students from disadvantaged backgrounds and female students in male-dominated fields
International students studying in a language other than their native one
Final-year students preparing a graduation thesis in a laboratory

mcq.q: Which slogan summarizes the constructivist approach in the discussion?
o: "Read, don't discuss"
"Tell, don't ask"
"Memorize, don't explain"
"Ask, don't tell"

o: Overt behaviors that students perform and teachers can see
Students' scores on final exams of the course in question
Physiological reactions such as heart rate and brain activity of students while learning
Interest levels reported by students on a questionnaire at the end of each session
mcq.e: The abstract: "the ICAP framework that defines cognitive engagement activities on the basis of students' overt behaviors".

mcq.q: What are the four modes of ICAP?
o: Interactive, Constructive, Active and Passive
Individual, Collaborative, Adaptive and Personalized
Imitative, Creative, Analytical and Practical
Intrinsic, Cognitive, Affective and Physical

mcq.q: What order of learning does the ICAP hypothesis predict?
o: Constructive greater than Interactive greater than Active greater than Passive
Passive greater than Active greater than Constructive greater than Interactive
All four modes give the same learning on every kind of task
Interactive greater than Constructive greater than Active greater than Passive (I > C > A > P)

mcq.q: How is "active learning" typically defined in educational research, per the paper?
o: Rapid learning driven by time pressure and competition among students
Learning based entirely on real-life experience without any reading of materials
Learning that occurs outside the classroom without the guidance of a teacher
Learning that requires students to engage cognitively and meaningfully with the materials
mcq.e: The paper: "'Active learning' is typically defined by educational researchers as learning that requires students to engage cognitively and meaningfully with the materials (Bonwell & Eison, 1991)".

o: Too few students enroll, too few instructors hold doctorates, too few large classrooms
Students object, parents object, administrators object to new methods
General advice does not say how to create activities, there are few criteria for choosing them
Too little teaching time, too little money for equipment, too few modern textbooks

mcq.q: Why does ICAP use overt behavior as an indicator?
o: It is the best noninvasive measure available
Because internal cognitive processes do not exist and do not affect learning
Because teachers are not permitted to ask students what they are thinking
Because overt behavior reflects every internal thought process with perfect accuracy

mcq.q: How do "learning activities" and "engagement activities" differ in the paper?
o: Learning tasks are what the teacher chooses for students to do
Learning tasks exist only in face-to-face classes and engagement only in online classes
The two terms mean the same thing and can be used interchangeably
Learning tasks are student behaviors while engagement is what the teacher chooses

o: Memory, attention and language of students in the classroom
Motivational, behavioral (attendance, homework) and emotional

mcq.q: How are instructional tasks related to engagement mode?
o: Orthogonal: with the same task such as reading, students can engage passively
Opposed: reading tasks are always passive and listening tasks always active
Unrelated: the teacher alone decides the mode of engagement, not the task
Fully dependent: each learning task allows exactly one mode of engagement

mcq.q: How is the passive mode defined?
o: Learners ask the instructor questions after the lecture has ended
Learners discuss the lecture with a friend while the instructor is speaking
Learners orient toward and receive information without overtly doing anything else related to learning
Learners copy the whole lecture in their own words into their notebooks

mcq.q: Which is an example of passive behavior?
o: Paying attention to a lecture without taking notes or doing anything else
Arguing with a friend to defend a position about the lesson
Drawing a concept map from a reading in one's own way
Underlining important sentences while reading a printed text

mcq.q: How is the active mode defined?
o: Some form of overt motoric action or physical manipulation is undertaken with the materials
Looking at the materials without performing any overt action
Taking turns in dialogue with a friend, both adding new ideas
Producing new output containing ideas beyond the learning materials
mcq.e: The paper: "Learners' engagement with instructional materials can be operationalized as active if some form of overt motoric action or physical manipulation is undertaken."

mcq.q: Which is an example of active behavior?
o: Explaining a solution step in one's own words beyond what the material says
Underlining important sentences, copying notes verbatim
Debating with a friend to defend a well-founded view about the lesson
Drawing a new concept map that is not in the original learning material

mcq.q: Why is reading a whole passage aloud closer to passive than active?
o: Because reading aloud makes no sound and so is not a motoric behavior
Because attention is not focused on specific sentences
Because reading aloud always tires students so they cannot learn much
Because reading aloud is not allowed in university classes

Learners generate or produce additional externalized output beyond what was provided in the materials
Learners listen to a partner's explanation and agree with short replies
Learners pick the correct answer from a list of options shown on a screen
mcq.e: The paper: "constructive behaviors as those in which learners generate or produce additional externalized outputs or products beyond what was provided in the learning materials."

mcq.q: Which is an example of constructive behavior?

Choosing the best matching image from a list of given images
Reading silently and watching a video without pausing or rewinding
Self-explaining, drawing concept maps, taking notes in one's own words

mcq.q: Which mode is a self-explanation copied verbatim from the material?

Passive, since the learner produces no externalized output at all
Active, since it provides no new information beyond the material
Interactive, since the learner interacts with the material itself

Copying the existing diagram is active

Passive, since no motoric action is involved
Constructive, since the respondent produces an answer

mcq.q: Which two criteria must the interactive mode satisfy?

Both partners primarily active, and at least one teacher taking part in the dialogue

Passive, since both only receive information from the other
Active, since they interact only through motoric action with no discourse
Interactive, since two students work together on the assignment

mcq.q: What is "individual dialogue"?
o: One partner dominates and makes most contributions while the other merely agrees
Each partner talking to himself or herself without listening to the other
Two partners both contributing fully and taking turns frequently
Two partners talking privately where no one else can hear them
mcq.e: The paper: "when one partner dominates and generates most of the substantive contributions and the other partner merely agrees... the 'speaker' may be learning more than his or her 'listening' partner... individual dialogue".

mcq.q: Why is joint dialogue more effective?
o: Because a teacher supervises to make sure every argument is correct
Because the partners always agree, so no time is wasted on pointless argument
Because joint dialogue is always shorter and saves time compared with individual dialogue
Both partners are constructive and take turns often
mcq.e: The paper: "by frequently taking turns, it will be easier for students to incorporate their partners' understanding of the domain and to make adjustments to their own mental model".

mcq.q: Is a computer system that requires a response from the learner always interactive by ICAP?
o: No; selecting an answer from a menu is only active
No; every computer system is only passive because it is not a person
Yes; if the system gives automatic feedback it is always interactive
Yes; every system that requires learner responses is interactive
mcq.e: The paper: "selecting is only active in our taxonomy in that the student does not generate a product... responses to a so-called interactive computer-based system can also be classified as passive, active, constructive, or interactive".

mcq.q: Who can the partner be in interactive dialogue?
o: A peer, teacher, parent or computer agent if it responds in a content-relevant way
Only a teacher with expertise in the content being learned
Only a family member of the learner who wants to help
Only a peer of the same age and level as the learner
mcq.e: The paper: "a learner talking with another person who can be a peer, a teacher, a parent, or computer agent (assuming the computer agent responds in a content-relevant way)."

mcq.q: Why does "interactive subsume constructive"?
o: Because in interactive dialogue both partners must be constructive
Because dialogue is always evaluated by the teacher against criteria
Because two people talking always speak longer than one person alone
Because dialogue always produces a written product that is kept for grading
mcq.e: The paper: "It is in this sense that interactive subsumes constructive."

mcq.q: What does the "hierarchy" assumption mean?
o: The four modes are independent and have no subsuming relation
Interactive subsumes constructive, constructive subsumes active, active subsumes passive
Passive subsumes active, active subsumes constructive, constructive subsumes interactive
Whichever mode comes first is always worse than the mode that comes after
mcq.e: The paper: "a higher mode subsumes a lower mode. That is, interactive behaviors subsume constructive behaviors, and constructive behaviors subsume active, and active behaviors subsume passive."

mcq.q: What does "intended versus enacted" mean?
o: Whatever the teacher intends, students necessarily carry out
Asking students to do a behavior does not guarantee they do it
Students always do exactly what the teacher asks in every activity
Intended behavior is always better than enacted behavior in every learning activity
mcq.e: The paper: "asking students to carry out a behavior does not guarantee that the expected behavior will actually be carried out in the intended way."

mcq.q: Which example shows a student turning a constructive task into an active one?
o: Asked to discuss with a friend, producing new ideas about the lesson
Asked to summarize, rewriting the content with an entirely new sentence structure
Asked to summarize, deleting irrelevant sentences and copying the rest (delete-and-copy)
Asked to read silently, doing nothing more than reading
mcq.e: The paper: "the student can reduce the task to an active one by summarizing using a delete-and-copy strategy".

mcq.q: Which advantages of externalizing output does the paper name?
o: Making lessons shorter and saving paper for teachers and students
Helping students avoid thinking deeply about the lesson content
Data for teachers, reduced memory load, new material to infer from
Ensuring every student earns the maximum score on the final exam
mcq.e: The paper names practical (performance data for teachers and researchers), cognitive (less memory demand), learning (outputs become new material; chance to monitor) and epistemic (commitment and ownership) advantages.

mcq.q: Why is problem solving hard to classify in ICAP?
o: Problem solving has no externalized output that can be observed
It depends on how a student does it: plugging into a formula is active
Problem solving is always interactive when two students work on it
Problem solving is always passive when a worked solution is provided
mcq.e: The paper: "solving an algebra problem can be classified as an active behavior when the student... merely applies the formula... (plug and chug). However, solving a novel or more difficult problem may be classified as constructive if a student has to rederive an equation".

mcq.q: What are the four knowledge-change processes for modes P, A, C, I?
o: Recall, Apply, Transfer, Co-create
Infer, Store, Integrate, Co-infer
Store, Integrate, Infer, Co-infer
Encode, Retrieve, Forget, Relearn
mcq.e: The paper: "Store... (passive). Integrate... (active). Infer... (constructive). Co-Infer... (interactive)."

mcq.q: How is new information stored in the passive mode?
o: Tightly linked to every existing schema so it is easy to apply to new situations
Together with new inferences that the learner generates while listening
It is not stored at all because the learner does nothing besides listening
In isolation, not integrated with prior knowledge, becoming "inert" knowledge
mcq.e: The paper: "isolated 'storing'... Storing information in an isolated way means that new knowledge is not integrated with existing or prior knowledge... 'inert' (Whitehead, 1929)".

mcq.q: What does Scardamalia's example of encapsulated knowledge show?
o: A student who read about clotting explained cuts healing from the text but
A student who read about clotting drew a complete diagram of the circulatory system
A student who read nothing explained clotting from everyday experience
A student who read about clotting explained it the same smooth way both times
mcq.e: The paper: the second answer "My theory is that when you get a cut the blood vessel that got cut dies and the heart stops sending blood..." shows "the student's old ideas were not integrated with the newly learned knowledge".

mcq.q: In the active mode, what do manipulations like highlighting cause?
o: Activation of a schema relevant to the emphasized material
Dialogue with a partner to develop ideas neither of them knew before
New inferences that go beyond the information in the original materials
Complete deletion of old prior knowledge to make room for new information
mcq.e: The paper: "Such emphases may cause learners to activate a body of knowledge... once a relevant schema is activated, learners can assimilate or integrate new information into the activated schema, allowing the learner to fill gaps in the schema".

mcq.q: What process do constructive behaviors often require?
o: Only memorizing information verbatim without changing any schema
Only choosing the correct answer from a list of ready options
Inferring, including revising, reorganizing and reflecting
Only listening to others explain without offering one's own view
mcq.e: The paper: "Constructive behaviors often require the processes of 'inferring' (e.g., induce, deduce, and abduce). Inferring also includes revising, repairing, reorganizing, and reflecting."

mcq.q: What is "co-inferring" in the interactive mode?
o: Both partners infer exactly the same thing at exactly the same time
Each partner infers and iterates with new input from the other, cumulatively
One partner infers while the other only listens and takes notes
Both partners argue to prove who is right rather than creating new ideas
mcq.e: The paper: "Co-Infer: Each learner infers new knowledge from activated and integrated knowledge and iteratively infers knowledge with new inputs from conversational partner(s)"; benefit "in a cumulative and spiraling way".

mcq.q: What are the cognitive outcomes for P, A, C, I?
o: Co-create, transfer, apply, recall
Recall, apply, transfer, co-create
Analyze, synthesize, evaluate, create
Understand, remember, forget, relearn
mcq.e: The paper: "Cognitive outcomes: Recall, Apply, Transfer, Co-create".

mcq.q: What levels of understanding correspond to P, A, C, I?
o: Shallow, shallow, deep, deep
Deepest, deep, shallow, minimal
Minimal, minimal, shallow, shallow
Minimal, shallow, deep, deepest
mcq.e: Table 2: "Minimal understanding, Shallow understanding, Deep understanding, Deepest understanding".

mcq.q: What can knowledge learned in the passive mode be used for?
o: Application to problems very different from those studied earlier
Recall in the same cue or context
Explaining brand-new concepts the learner has never met
Transfer to distant domains to create novel ideas
mcq.e: The paper: "Such isolated storing is adequate for learning that does not require integration with prior knowledge, such as learning a specific procedure of how to operate an ATM machine."

mcq.q: What does the change from a "single-loop" to a "double-loop" circulatory model illustrate?
o: Mechanical copying of information in the active mode when taking verbatim notes
Confusion of concepts because dialogue between two friends was ineffective
Accommodation in knowledge, achieved through constructive engagement such as self-explaining
Isolated storing of new information in the passive mode when listening
mcq.e: The paper: "One example of accommodation is the change from conceiving of the human circulatory system as a 'single-loop' to a 'double-loop' model (Chi et al., 1994)... from constructively engaging with the materials (e.g., self-explaining)."

mcq.q: What does "the same set of knowledge-change processes" assume?
o: Different activities within a mode (underlining
Every mode uses exactly the same single knowledge-change process
Only the interactive mode has knowledge-change processes and the others do not
Each activity within a mode has entirely different knowledge-change processes
mcq.e: The paper: "although the types of activities within each mode may be different... their underlying knowledge-change processes are the same... underlining... focus attention... deleting irrelevant sentences... focus attention".

mcq.q: Which conditions did the four-mode study (Menekse, Stump, Krause and Chi 2013) compare?
o: Four groups of students listening to four instructors teach the same content
Reading the text (passive), reading and highlighting (active)
Four ways of reading the same passage with equal reading time
Four types of tests taken one after another by the same group of students
mcq.e: The paper: "reading a text passage (passive); reading and highlighting important sentences within the text (active); interpreting a graph... without having read the text passage (constructive); and interpreting the same graph jointly with a peer (interactive)."

mcq.q: What was the result of the four-mode study?
o: Learning improved significantly at about 8% to 10% across each mode, supporting ICAP
Learning rose exactly 50% in the interactive mode over the other three
Learning did not differ among the four modes on any type of question
The passive mode gave the highest result and the interactive mode the lowest
mcq.e: The paper: "These results support the ICAP hypothesis and show that learning improves significantly at a rate of around 8% to 10% across each mode."

mcq.q: How did easy multiple-choice questions behave in that study?
o: There were no easy items in the test of this study
Performance was the same for all modes; differences emerged only on more challenging items
The passive mode always did best on easy items since the text was read carefully
Differences were largest on easy items and absent on hard items
mcq.e: The paper: "performance on easy multiple-choice questions was the same for all levels of engagement activities, but condition differences emerged on more challenging assessment items."

mcq.q: How did Coleman, Brown and Rivkin (1997) classify the three roles?
o: Listening (passive), summarizing (constructive), explaining (interactive)
Listening (constructive), summarizing (passive), explaining (active)
Listening (active), summarizing (interactive), explaining (constructive)
Listening (passive), summarizing (active), explaining (constructive)
mcq.e: The paper: listening "passive", summarizing "active because... in many of the summaries participants did not go beyond the given text", explaining "constructive".

mcq.q: Why was the Coleman study not classified as interactive even though participants prepared "to teach"?
o: Because the study took place in a laboratory rather than in a classroom
Because while teaching, their partners were told only to listen
Because the study did not measure participants' transfer performance
Because participants worked alone with no fellow students at all
mcq.e: The paper: "we do not consider this an interactive activity because while teaching, their partners were instructed only to listen and not ask questions."

mcq.q: What did Gobert and Clement (1999) on plate tectonics find?
o: Drawing diagrams from text (constructive) beat writing summaries (active)
Only reading the text beat writing summaries, which beat drawing diagrams
The three groups performed equivalently with no significant differences
Writing summaries beat drawing diagrams on both spatial and causal knowledge
mcq.e: The paper: "the constructive (diagram) group did better on both measures of spatial and causal knowledge than the active (summary) group did, which in turn did better than the passive reading group."

mcq.q: Which note-taking style is classified as constructive?
o: Copying and pasting short segments of the target text with a computer tool
Copying the entire material verbatim because it shows the learner's diligence
Notes in one's own words, because the summary may include conclusions and inferences
Reading the text without writing any notes into the notebook
mcq.e: The paper: "take notes in their own words (which is often constructive because the summary may include conclusions and inferences)."

mcq.q: What did Bauer and Koedinger (2007) find about notes?
o: Taking no notes was more effective than both free-form notes and cut-and-paste
Free-form notes and cut-and-paste did not differ at all in outcomes
Cut-and-paste was more effective than free-form notes because it is more accurate
Free-form notes (constructive) were more effective than cutting
mcq.e: The paper: "taking free-form notes (constructive) is more effective than cutting and pasting short segments of the target text (active; Bauer & Koedinger, 2007)."

mcq.q: Bauer and Koedinger found no difference between interface highlighting and cut-and-paste. Why does ICAP explain this?
o: Both are constructive, so they gave completely identical results
Both are interactive, so both reached the highest outcomes
Both are passive, so students learned nothing in either condition
Both are active, encouraging students to physically select without generating or integrating information
mcq.e: The paper: "This finding is expected according to the ICAP hypothesis because both are active activities that encourage students to physically select but not generate or integrate the information."

mcq.q: What did the collaborative note-taking study of Kam and colleagues (2005) find?
o: Collaborators took better notes (more reflections and questions)
Collaborators learned clearly better with a statistically highly significant difference
Solo note takers took better notes and learned better than collaborators
Collaborators and solo note takers did not differ in any respect
mcq.e: The paper: "Students who worked collaboratively were more likely to include reflections and pose questions... However, the small sample size in their classroom study was insufficient to observe any significant learning differences".

mcq.q: What did Yin and colleagues (2005) compare in concept mapping?
o: Selecting links (constructive) beat generating link labels (active) in accuracy
Generating and selecting links gave completely equal results on every index
Generating link labels (constructive) beat selecting links to complete the map (active) in accuracy and structural complexity
Reading a ready map (passive) beat both generating and selecting links
mcq.e: The paper: "students who were asked to generate the labels for the links on a concept map (constructive) did better in total accuracy and map structure complexity than students who were asked to select the links to complete the concept map (active)."

mcq.q: What did Czerniak and Haney (1998) show about concept maps?
o: Building maps collaboratively (interactive) beat listening to lectures
Building maps alone beat building with a friend because of fewer distractions
Lectures beat both building maps alone and building maps with a friend
Concept maps gave no benefit compared with ordinary lectures
mcq.e: The paper: "collaboratively building concept maps (interactive) results in better learning than just listening to a lecture... Collaboratively building maps is also better than individually creating maps".

mcq.q: What did Hausmann and colleagues (2008) compare in self-explaining?
o: Explaining with a partner and alone gave no difference in results
Self-explaining while rereading was worse than rereading without explaining
Explaining alone versus explaining with a partner; alone was better for focus
Explaining with a partner versus explaining alone; with a partner was better
mcq.e: Table 5: "Explain with partner > Explain alone (Hausmann et al., 2008)".

mcq.q: Which mode was the Deslauriers, Schelew and Wieman (2011) classroom study classified as, and what was the result?
o: Interactive (peer discussion); it produced more learning than traditional lecture
Constructive (individual tasks only); it produced less learning than only reading
Passive (mostly lecturing); it produced less learning than traditional lecture
Active (only clickers); it produced the same learning as traditional lecture
mcq.e: The paper: the intervention included "predicting, reasoning, solving, critiquing, and peer discussion. We classify this intervention as an interactive one because it includes peer-to-peer discussion. As predicted, the intervention promoted more learning than listening to traditional lectures."

mcq.q: What does the Zhang and Linn (2013) chemical reactions study illustrate?
o: The two pairs learned equally because both worked with a partner
The pair choosing given images learned better because they made fewer errors together
Both pairs worked together, but only the pair drawing molecules (constructive) was interactive
The pair drawing molecules learned worse because drawing took time and distracted
mcq.e: The paper: "simply asking students to work together does not automatically make an activity interactive... only the generate condition can be considered interactive... interactive activities require partners to be constructive".

mcq.q: What did classroom studies by Dockter and colleagues (2010) and Whitten (2011) show about adding constructive activity to problem solving?
o: Adding a constructive activity reduced learning by overloading students
Adding a constructive activity had no effect compared with solving alone
Adding a constructive activity helped only students who were already very strong
Adding a constructive activity such as compare
mcq.e: The paper: "two studies compared problem-solving alone... to solving problems with an added constructive activity (such as compare and contrast... and responding to guided prompts...). The results showed that adding the constructive activity improves learning."

mcq.q: Which three factors can override ICAP's predictions?
o: Assessment measures, domain, and task differences within a mode
Tuition, school location and number of female students in the class
Language of instruction, color of materials and time of day of the class
Teacher age, class size and weekly hours of students
mcq.e: The paper: "three factors that can override the predictions of the ICAP hypothesis": "Assessment measures", "Domain", "Task differences within a mode".

mcq.q: Why can shallow assessments hide ICAP differences?
o: Shallow questions always have several correct answers and cannot be scored
Recall-only questions can be answered by passive reception
Shallow questions are used only with elementary pupils, not university students
Shallow questions are so hard that no student answers correctly in any mode
mcq.e: The paper: "performance on shallow or easy assessment questions typically is not sensitive to various intervention efforts... because shallow questions that require only recall of information can be answered with passive receiving type of activities."

mcq.q: What did Aleven and Koedinger (2002) find when prompting students to explain while solving geometry problems?
o: The same advantage on all items whether easy or hard
No advantage on any type of item on the test
No advantage on easy-to-guess items but clear benefits on hard-to-guess and transfer items
Clear advantage on easy-to-guess items but none on hard-to-guess and transfer items
mcq.e: The paper: "no advantage for explanation on easy-to-guess items but significant benefits of explanation for hard-to-guess and transfer problems."

mcq.q: What kind of domain does the English article system example represent, where ICAP may fail?
o: A mathematics domain with strict logical rules that can be proved
A history domain with many events that can be inferred causally
A science domain with many experiments to test hypotheses directly
A procedural domain with arbitrary human-made rules
mcq.e: The paper: "simple procedural domains for which the rules are arbitrary and cannot be logically deduced. For example, the English article system... governed by a complicated set of human-made rules and exceptions".

mcq.q: What difficulty does the concept of "emergence" illustrate?
o: A topic so short that there is no time for interactive activities
A topic so novel that students lack relevant schemas to bootstrap deeper understanding, even with constructive activities
A topic so old that students have memorized it and need no more inference
A topic so easy that constructive activities are not needed to learn it well
mcq.e: The paper: "concept of emergence... a novel idea that many students do not have relevant or related knowledge to understand... constructive activities... help students learn only the basic detailed information... not the interlevel causal relationships".

mcq.q: What did Chi and colleagues (2012) on horizontal projectile motion compare?
o: Two passive activities, reading versus listening; the reading group learned more
Two interactive activities, inventing a method versus comparing and contrasting
Two constructive activities, drawing and writing; the two groups learned equally
An interactive and a passive activity; the passive group learned more
mcq.e: The paper: "Students in the invent condition showed greater learning gains compared to students in the compare–contrast condition, even though both conditions are interactive."

mcq.q: What did worksheet analysis show about the two groups?
o: Both groups made the same number of triple-feature and single-feature statements
100% of the invent group made triple-feature statements versus 10% of the compare group
10% of the invent group made triple-feature statements versus 100% of the compare group
The invent group made only single-feature statements like the compare group
mcq.e: The paper: "only 10% of the compare–contrast group produced triple-feature statements, whereas 100% of the invent group did... the compare–contrast group produced on average 3.0 single-feature statements, whereas the invention groups produced no single-feature statements."

mcq.q: How does ICAP explain "discrepant" findings about note taking or summarizing?
o: The discrepant results are simply statistical errors by the researchers
Note taking and summarizing are equally effective however they are implemented
Note taking and summarizing never work because they only waste learners' time
Effectiveness depends on how it is implemented, what it is compared with
mcq.e: The paper: "whether note taking is an effective learning activity depends on three factors: (a) how it is implemented... (b) what the alternative (or often the control) condition... (c) how students actually carried out the activity."

mcq.q: What do Mastropieri and colleagues (2001) and Coleman and colleagues (1997) illustrate about summarizing?
o: Summarizing always loses to reading aloud however it is done
Summarizing by selecting sentences beat summarizing by explaining in both studies
Summarizing by answering questions (constructive) beat reading aloud (passive)
Summarizing always beats every other activity however it is done
mcq.e: The paper: "Thus, it is not surprising that learning is better in the constructive summarizing case (Mastropieri et al., 2001)... summarization through selection (active) is worse for learning than summarizing through explanation (constructive; Coleman et al., 1997)."

mcq.q: How does ICAP recommend choosing a control for the most stringent comparison?
o: Compare the intervention with a condition with more resources to raise statistical power
Compare the intervention with a passive condition so the effect is as large as possible
Compare the intervention with another intervention using an activity of the same mode of engagement
Compare the intervention with a do-nothing condition to show its effect most clearly
mcq.e: The paper: "the most stringent comparison of an intervention is to compare it with another intervention that employs an engagement activity of the same mode."

mcq.q: What does the metacognitive prompt example illustrate?
o: Metacognitive prompts work only when compared with doing nothing at all
Metacognitive prompts need no control group because the benefit is obvious
Metacognitive prompts always work better than any other intervention
To claim a prompt is useful, compare it with another prompt that also elicits generative responses, not with reading advice that elicits none
mcq.e: The paper: "to claim that inserting a metacognitive prompt is a useful intervention... one needs to compare it with another type of prompt that also elicits generative responses so that both activities are constructive, rather than comparing it with reading academic advice that does not elicit a response."

mcq.q: Which modes do most studies in Tables 3 to 5 compare?
o: All four modes compared evenly with equal numbers of studies
Interactive with passive; far fewer compare interactive with constructive
Active with passive; far fewer compare active with constructive
Constructive with passive; far fewer compare constructive with active
mcq.e: The paper: "the majority of the studies on interventions compared a constructive mode with a passive mode. Far fewer studies have compared the constructive mode with active, interactive, or other constructive modes."

mcq.q: Why should "active learning" not be read as any activity students do?
o: Because Freeman proved that only group work counts as active learning
Because all student activities raise deep understanding equally under ICAP
Because active learning includes only activities chosen beforehand by the instructor
Because in ICAP verbatim copying or menu choosing is still active
mcq.e: Chi and Wylie: verbatim copying and menu choosing are active; constructive needs output "beyond the information given".

mcq.q: Why is telling students to "work in groups" not enough for interaction in ICAP?
o: Because groups work only when an instructor sits with the group all session
Real interaction needs both partners constructive with frequent turn taking
Because ICAP does not recognize group work as a form of learning
Because group work always lowers learning compared with individual work
mcq.e: Chi and Wylie: "simply asking students to work together does not automatically make an activity interactive... to be interactive, students must work together on a constructive task."

mcq.q: Why should 0.47 SD not be treated as absolute causal proof?
o: Because the meta-analysis used only unpublished studies, which cannot be trusted
Because 0.47 is below the threshold of accepted practical significance
Most studies were not randomized (only 16 randomized or crossover)
Because Freeman's meta-analysis was retracted after errors in the data were found
mcq.e: Freeman: Table 1 shows n = 16 randomized or crossover studies; instructors were volunteers; intensity could not be evaluated. No failure-rate study was fully randomized.

mcq.q: Do Freeman and Chi–Wylie discuss generative AI?
o: Yes; both papers contain a section on learning with generative AI
Only Freeman discusses AI, while Chi and Wylie do not
Only Chi and Wylie discuss AI, while Freeman does not
No; every link to AI in the thesis is design inference needing testing
mcq.e: Both papers were published in 2014, before the wave of generative AI; links to AI are my design inference.

mcq.q: Under ICAP, which mode is a student copying or choosing the AI's ready answer (design inference)?
o: Interactive, since there was a dialogue between student and AI when receiving the answer
Active or even passive, since no output beyond the given information is produced
No mode, since ICAP does not apply to software
Constructive, since the student interacted with the AI and got an answer
mcq.e: Inference from ICAP definitions: copying or choosing a ready answer is active/passive; dialogue is interactive only when both sides contribute new ideas (the AI counts as a partner if it responds content-relevantly).

mcq.q: When could AI use approach the constructive or interactive mode (design inference)?
o: When students self-explain, write pseudocode, ask questions beyond the material
When students use the AI to check the spelling in their report
When students skim the AI's answer and move on to the next question
When students ask the AI to write all the source code and hand it in unedited
mcq.e: Inference from ICAP: behavior determines the mode, not the tool; constructive needs output beyond the material, interactive needs alternating constructive contributions from both sides.

mcq.q: If the "free AI use" control mostly receives answers and the treatment forces constructive work, what could explain a difference (design inference)?
o: Certainly the responsible AI raising the innate ability of the students
The mode of engagement (constructive versus active or passive)
No difference is possible since both groups use AI in the same way
Certainly the treatment group having better students from the start
mcq.e: Chi and Wylie advise the most stringent comparison is between same-mode interventions; with different modes, the effect may come from the mode rather than from the specific features of the intervention.

mcq.q: From Chi and Wylie, how should effects be measured in the thesis (design inference)?
o: Use only recall multiple-choice items, which are easy to score and compare across groups
Use only self-report questionnaires about how engaged students felt in the lesson
Use hard and transfer items, and analyze products or interaction logs to learn the actual enacted mode
Use only the number of logins to the system as an indicator of deep learning
mcq.e: Chi and Wylie: shallow items are insensitive to interventions; intended and enacted behavior differ, so products need analyzing.

mcq.q: What is an important limitation of Freeman (2014) as a base for a thesis on programming with AI?
o: It concerns in-class active learning in university STEM before generative AI
It never mentions any computer science or mathematics course at all
It measured only student satisfaction and never measured actual scores
It had only 10 students so it has no statistical meaning for the thesis
mcq.e: Freeman pooled 225 STEM studies (2014) of in-class active learning; it says nothing about AI. Generalizing to programming with AI is inference to be tested (Module 13).

essay.q: Present the main results of Freeman and colleagues (2014): the exam effect, the odds ratio and failure rates. Give two practical interpretations by the authors and two limitations.
essay.m: Hint: 0.47 SD from 158 studies; OR 1.95 (RR 1.5) from 67 studies; failure 21.8% versus 33.8% (a 55% increase). Interpretations: 50th to 68th percentile; scores about 6% higher and 0.3 final-grade points; 3,516 fewer failing students (about US$3.5 million tuition). Limits: volunteer instructors; no intensity data; most studies not randomized; the medical trial analogy is qualified.

essay.q: Analyze the robustness of Freeman's conclusions: discipline, class size, design quality, publication bias; then say how far you trust them for a programming class.
essay.m: Hint: No difference by discipline (P = 0.160 and 0.068); small classes (50 or fewer) benefit most; randomized g = 0.514 does not differ from quasi-random; fail-safe 114 and 438; smaller effect with instructor exams than concept inventories. Trust: fairly good for STEM in general, but programming with AI needs its own test; the paper has no AI data.

essay.q: Explain the ICAP framework: the four modes, the knowledge-change process and the cognitive outcome of each. Give one programming example per mode.
essay.m: Hint: Passive (store, recall; watching a code walkthrough video); active (integrate, apply; copying or choosing sample code, underlining); constructive (infer, transfer; self-explaining code, writing pseudocode, designing own test cases); interactive (co-infer, co-create; two students or a student and an AI take turns adding new ideas to design an algorithm). State the subsuming hierarchy I > C > A > P. Examples are design inference.

essay.q: State the conditions for a dialogue to be "interactive" in Chi and Wylie and distinguish joint from individual dialogue. Apply this to a student's Q and A with an AI.
essay.m: Hint: Both partners primarily constructive and turn taking frequent enough. Individual dialogue: one talks, the other says "uh-huh", mainly the speaker learns. Application: if the student only asks and copies the answer it is active/passive; if the student offers hypotheses, objects, revises a solution and the AI responds content-relevantly it approaches joint dialogue. Logs must be analyzed to learn the enacted mode (intended versus enacted).

essay.q: Name three factors that can make ICAP fail and give one remedy for each when designing tests and the control group in your thesis.
essay.m: Hint: Assessment (shallow items insensitive: use hard and transfer items); domain (arbitrary rules or too-novel topics: choose content where students have prior schemas, e.g. syntax versus algorithms); task within a mode (invent and compare are both interactive but differ in outcome: describe tasks precisely, compare same-mode interventions, analyze products). The control should be the same mode if you want to isolate the effect of "responsible AI".

essay.q: Propose how your thesis could use Freeman and ICAP to defend the treatment group (Socratic AI), while stating the limits you must not claim.
essay.m: Hint: Freeman: pooled evidence that active learning raises scores and cuts failure in STEM (0.47 SD; OR 1.95); ICAP: mechanism and design (constructive/interactive over active/passive). Defense: the treatment forces students to predict, explain and reflect, so it is constructive. Limits: neither paper covers generative AI; first-generation studies with volunteer instructors; the effect need not carry over to programming with AI; a dedicated experiment is required (Module 13).
